level: In-depth engineering course · no official exam
name: Application Security for Web and LLM Apps
audience: Engineers and architects who build and run web products and AI features and must keep them secure without a dedicated security team.
format: This site's course with a 40-question practice test of find-the-vulnerability, choose-the-control, read-the-config and incident questions.
scenarios: Reviewing a pull request for security bugs
Designing authentication and authorization for a SaaS
Shipping an LLM feature that reads user documents
Preparing for a customer security questionnaire
verifyNotes: This is the site's own in-depth engineering course, not a vendor certification: there are no exam facts to confirm, so spend Research on finding the best official/primary sources per topic (URLs that will be cited as sources) and on what is current as of November 2026. Goal: a senior engineer or architect who builds products alone or in a team of 2-3 can apply every idea confidently in real work, a design review or a senior interview. Lessons go deep: intuition first, then the precise mechanism, then a fully worked example with real numbers or code, then where it matters in production, then a common misconception. Write math in LaTeX between double dollars only: $$...$$; NEVER single-dollar math (single $ renders literally; in SQL or shell code use code fences). In JSON strings escape backslashes. Markdown tables: never put a raw | inside a cell (escape it as \\| or use \\lvert in math). Every lesson has a hands-on lab: a small exercise with the expected output. State any randomness seed. Code in fenced blocks with the right language. Question mix: ~35% find-the-vulnerability in code or config (TypeScript/Node, SQL, HTTP headers, CSP, OAuth flows, prompts and tool definitions), ~35% choose-the-control (the simplest effective fix a small team can run), ~30% threat-modelling and incident reasoning. Verifiers MUST type-check every TypeScript/TSX example with `sh /Users/ashotpahlevanyan/MyProjects/maark/claude-cert/web/.pipeline/ts/check.sh <file>` (TypeScript 7.0 strict, Node 24; set NORUN=1 for .tsx or code that needs network; installed: zod 4, react 19, react-native 0.88 types, next 16, vitest 5, @modelcontextprotocol/sdk 1.32, @anthropic-ai/sdk 1.3, jose 6). Run every SQL example with `node /Users/ashotpahlevanyan/MyProjects/maark/claude-cert/web/.pipeline/sql/run.mjs <file.sql>` (PostgreSQL 18 via PGlite, pgvector and pg_trgm available). Run every Python example and compute every number with /Users/ashotpahlevanyan/MyProjects/maark/claude-cert/web/.pipeline/py313/bin/python (CPython 3.13 + PyYAML) or /Users/ashotpahlevanyan/MyProjects/maark/claude-cert/web/.pipeline/py/bin/python (numpy, pandas, scipy, scikit-learn). Never include working exploit chains against real products; show vulnerable and fixed code side by side on toy apps. Verify headers, cookies and CSP against MDN and the W3C/WHATWG specs; OAuth against RFC 9700 (OAuth 2.0 Security BCP) and the OAuth 2.1 draft; passwords against NIST SP 800-63B and OWASP cheat sheets; LLM risks against the OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications 2025 and the OWASP agentic security guidance. OWASP Top 10:2025 is the current web edition. Version-sensitive facts must be dated. Sources: owasp.org, cheatsheetseries.owasp.org, genai.owasp.org, developer.mozilla.org, w3.org, whatwg.org, rfc-editor.org, ietf.org, oauth.net, openid.net, nist.gov (csrc.nist.gov, pages.nist.gov), cwe.mitre.org, cve.org, cisa.gov, docs.github.com (secret scanning, Dependabot, code scanning), slsa.dev, openssf.org, nodejs.org, postgresql.org, platform.claude.com and developers.openai.com for LLM-provider guidance; no Medium or vendor-marketing blogs.

domains.name: Threat modelling and secure design
skills: Threat modelling a small product: data-flow diagrams, trust boundaries, STRIDE, and ranking by likelihood and impact
Secure defaults and least privilege across app, database and cloud
Security requirements for a small team: OWASP ASVS levels and what to do first
Logging and monitoring for security: what to log, what never to log, alerting on abuse
Security in the delivery flow: reviews, SAST, dependency and secret scanning without drowning in noise

domains.name: Authentication and sessions
skills: Passwords done right per NIST SP 800-63B: length over complexity, breached-password checks, argon2id/bcrypt hashing and rate limiting
Passkeys and WebAuthn, MFA options and account recovery that is not the weakest link
Session management: cookie attributes (HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite, __Host- prefix), rotation, expiry and logout
OAuth 2.0 / OpenID Connect for apps: authorization code with PKCE, redirect URI rules, state and nonce, token storage in browsers and mobile
JWTs: when to use them, algorithm confusion, validation of iss/aud/exp, revocation strategies

domains.name: Authorization and data protection
skills: Broken access control: IDOR/BOLA, missing function-level checks, and tenant isolation in multi-tenant SaaS
Authorization models: RBAC, ABAC and relationship-based; enforcing in one place; Postgres row-level security
Data protection: encryption in transit and at rest, key management, field-level encryption for secrets and PII
Secrets management: never in code or images, rotation, short-lived credentials, responding to a leak
Privacy engineering basics: minimisation, retention, deletion and audit trails

domains.name: Injection and browser security
skills: SQL and NoSQL injection, command injection and safe query building; ORMs are not automatic protection
Cross-site scripting: contexts, output encoding, sanitising HTML, framework escape hatches like dangerouslySetInnerHTML
Content Security Policy: nonces and hashes, strict-dynamic, reporting, and why unsafe-inline undermines it
CSRF and SameSite cookies, CORS misconfigurations, clickjacking and frame-ancestors
Server-side request forgery, path traversal, unsafe deserialisation and file upload handling

domains.name: LLM and agent application security
skills: OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications 2025 applied to a real feature
Prompt injection, direct and indirect: why it cannot be fully filtered, and architectural mitigations (privilege separation, untrusted-content labelling, human approval, egress limits)
Sensitive data in LLM apps: leakage through prompts, logs, retrieval permissions and model providers' data policies
Insecure output handling: rendering model output as HTML/Markdown, executing model-written code or SQL, tool argument validation
Securing RAG and agents: document-level permissions at retrieval time, tool scopes, MCP server trust

domains.name: Supply chain, infrastructure and incident response
skills: Dependency risk: lockfiles, audits, typosquatting, install scripts, and update policies with Dependabot
Build integrity: SLSA levels, provenance and artifact attestations, pinning CI actions
Cloud and container hardening basics: IAM, public buckets, non-root containers, network exposure
Security headers and TLS configuration: HSTS, cookies, referrer policy, permissions policy
Incident response for a small team: detect, contain, rotate, notify (including breach-notification duties), and the postmortem
